title: Internal Link Audit: Ecommerce Content Cluster
description: The internal-link audit process for a 28-page ecommerce content cluster: how to find orphans, fix broken anchors, rebalance authority, and verify the structure.
ogTitle: Internal Link Audit: Ecommerce Content Cluster
ogDescription: The repeatable process for auditing internal links across a 28-page content cluster, with specific steps and checklists.
h1: Internal Link Audit: The Complete Process for an Ecommerce Content Cluster

inline: the operations checklist for auditing the internal linking of a large ecommerce content cluster — in this case, the 28-page cluster built over the previous 28 days. Every step below can be done in a single working day, and the result is a cluster where every page is reachable within three clicks of the homepage, every key page has adequate internal link authority, and no page is orphaned.

This is not an SEO theory page. It is the exact process we use to audit and fix a cluster after it has been built, and it assumes you have already published the 28 pages from this roadmap. If you are still building the cluster, this page can wait — do the audit on the day of publication, not before.

sections.title: Why an Internal Link Audit Matters

inline: A cluster of 28 pages with poor internal linking is not a cluster — it is 28 pages that happen to share a topic. What makes it a cluster is the internal linking structure that tells Google which pages are the hubs, which are the spokes, and which pages are the most important within the topic. Google reads internal linking as an editorial signal: pages with more internal links pointing to them are treated as more important.

items: Pages with no internal links pointing to them, which Google may not crawl or may treat as low-priority.
Internal links pointing to pages that do not exist or have moved. These waste crawl budget and confuse Google.
Every page linking to another page with the same anchor text — which looks manipulative and dilutes rather than strengthens the signal.
Pages that should be important (the pillar, the geo hub, the case study) not receiving enough internal links, while peripheral pages receive too many.
Pages that require more than three clicks from the homepage, which reduces their crawl frequency and search visibility.

blocks.text: What an audit does not fix

inline: An internal link audit does not fix weak content, poor search intent matching, or low domain authority. It is a

optimization — important for making the cluster function, but not a substitute for the content itself being good. If a page is not performing, and the internal linking is already correct, the problem is almost certainly the content or the intent match.

Ideally the audit is done on the day the cluster is published, before any significant amount of time has passed. Google will have already crawled some of the pages, and the internal linking corrections will feed into the next crawl. It is much easier to fix structural issues early than after the cluster has been live for months.
The audit below is sequential — each step depends on the one before it. Do them in order.
Total: roughly 4 hours for a single audit pass. For a 28-page cluster, this is one working day, including time to fix the issues as they are found.
Start by crawling the entire site, not just the cluster. The crawl gives you a complete picture of every page, every link, and every issue.

inline: An orphan page is a page that has no internal links pointing to it. Orphans are bad for two reasons: Google may not crawl them (because nothing links to them), and even if Google does crawl them (via sitemap), they receive no internal authority and rank poorly.

items: Reports → Crawl Analysis → Orphan URLs (requires connecting to Google Analytics or Search Console for full accuracy).
For each page in the sitemap, search the crawl output for internal links pointing to it. If zero, it is an orphan.

blocks.text: Common orphan patterns in a cluster

b: Hub pages that were never linked from the homepage.

items: The geo hub and the glossary are particularly vulnerable if they were not added to the main navigation.
The brief template may have its download link, but the page itself may be orphaned if nothing links to it.
The case study may only be linked from the portfolio page, which itself may not be linked from the homepage.
The reviews page may only be linked from the portfolio page, which means it is effectively orphaned.
Add links to the top-level hubs (pillar, geo hub, portfolio, reviews, glossary) from the homepage.
Every orphan page should be linked from at least one related cluster page.
The XML sitemap should include all pages, but sitemap inclusion is not a substitute for internal linking — it just tells Google the page exists.

inline: The pages most at risk of being orphaned are:

items: The city pages — linked only from the geo hub and each other.
The geo hub — linked only from the city pages and the near-me guide.
The glossary — linked only from wherever you add it, which may be nowhere.
The internal-link audit (this page) — linked only from the pages it describes.

inline: Verify each of those has at least two inbound internal links from within the cluster before moving to the next step.

Broken internal links are 404s (page not found) or 500s (server error). They waste crawl budget, they confuse Google, and they frustrate readers. Every internal link in the cluster should resolve to a 200 status code, without a redirect chain.

items: Response Codes → Client Error (4xx) — these are broken links.
Response Codes → Redirection (3xx) — these are redirects, which should be replaced with direct links.

blocks.text: Common broken-link patterns in this cluster

items: Links like /ecommerce-developer-contract-payment-terms/#change-orders fail if the target page does not have an element with that ID. Every anchor fragment must have a matching ID on the target page.
If a page URL changed between draft and publication, older links may still point to the old URL.
If a page in the cluster was not published (e.g., if you skipped a day), links to it are broken.
Manual link insertion can produce typos that do not surface until the crawl.

b: Update the link to the correct URL.

items: Preferred fix — internal links should point directly to the final destination.
If a fragment link fails because the target page lacks an element with that ID, add the ID to the target page.
If the original URL should never be used again, redirect it. But internal links should still point to the final URL, not to the redirect.
If the target page genuinely does not exist and should not, remove the link rather than leaving it broken.

inline: Every fragment link (e.g., #change-orders) requires a matching element ID on the target page. This cluster uses a lot of fragment links — the contract page, the process page, the near-me guide, and the cost page all have fragment anchors referenced from multiple pages. Verify every one of them by checking the target page's HTML.

Anchor text — the visible text of a link — tells Google what the target page is about. The ideal pattern is: one exact-match anchor per important page, several partial and semantic anchors, and no anchor repeated dozens of times. This pattern looks natural and produces the strongest signal.

items: Bulk Export → Inlinks → export a spreadsheet with columns: Source URL, Destination URL, Anchor Text.
This shows every anchor pointing to each page.
If the same anchor appears 20+ times pointing to the same page, that is excessive.

inline: Internal linking distributes authority — the more internal links pointing to a page, the more "important" it seems to Google. In a well-structured cluster, authority flows from peripheral pages toward the hubs, not the other way around. The hubs (pillar, geo hub, portfolio) should have the most inbound internal links.

The goal is a reasonable distribution, not a perfect one. If the pillar has 40 internal links and the glossary has 8, that is healthy. If the pillar has 12 and the glossary has 8, that is a problem.

inline: For each gap, add the missing cross-link at the natural place in the content — not in a "related posts" block at the end. Contextual links in the body text are worth more than a footer widget. If a natural place does not exist, edit the content to create one.

Schema and canonical tags are not internal links, but they play a similar role — they tell Google which page is the canonical version and what the page is about. A cluster with correct schema and canonicals is much easier for Google to interpret than one without.

b: Every page has a self-referencing canonical.

items: The <link rel="canonical"> tag should point to the page's own URL, not to another page.

items: Unless the page is intentionally a duplicate (e.g., a paginated version), canonicals should be self-referencing.

☐ No orphan pages — every page has at least two inbound internal links.
☐ Every page is at depth 3 or less from the homepage.

☐ All fragment links (e.g., #change-orders) have matching element IDs on their target pages.
☐ Every page has a self-referencing canonical tag.
☐ Every page with a visible FAQ has FAQPage schema matching the visible content.
☐ No page has hidden FAQ schema (schema without visible matching content).
☐ XML sitemap includes all 28 cluster pages, with correct lastmod dates.
☐ robots.txt does not block any cluster page.
☐ Google Search Console shows all 28 pages indexed (or in the process of being indexed).

inline: If any of these are not satisfied, fix them before considering the audit complete. Most take a few minutes; the whole checklist should take 30–60 minutes after the 8 steps are done.

Internal linking is not a one-time task. As the site grows and new pages are added, the internal link structure needs to evolve with it. The audit should be repeated on a regular cadence, and additionally whenever new content is added.

faqs.q: How long does an internal link audit take?
a: For a 28-page cluster, the 8 steps take roughly 4 hours, and the final checklist takes 30–60 minutes. Total: about one working day. The initial crawl takes the longest (30 min); everything else is faster once the tools are set up.

faqs.q: What is the most common issue found in an audit like this?
a: Broken fragment links and orphan pages. Fragment links fail because the target page does not have an element with the expected ID. Orphans happen when a page is published without being linked from anywhere — common for the glossary and the reviews page in a large cluster.

faqs.q: Do I need paid tools to do an audit?
a: No. Screaming Frog's free tier (up to 500 URLs) covers everything needed for a 28-page cluster. Ahrefs is useful but not required. Google Search Console (free) is essential for indexing verification.

faqs.q: How many internal links per page is too many?
a: There is no hard limit, but 100+ internal links per page is usually a sign of a menu-heavy or widget-heavy design, not a well-structured article. For cluster pages, 5–15 contextual internal links is a healthy range. Footer and navigation links are separate from this count.

faqs.q: Should I use "nofollow" on internal links?
a: Rarely. Nofollow on internal links wastes the linking opportunity and is usually a sign of confusion about how nofollow works. Use nofollow only for links to genuinely low-value pages (e.g., privacy policy, terms of service) — and even then, follow is usually fine.

faqs.q: What is the difference between click depth and internal link count?
a: Click depth is the shortest path from the homepage to a page. Internal link count is the total number of pages linking to a page. Both matter, but they measure different things — a page can have high internal link count and high click depth (if all its inbound links come from deep pages), which is a structural problem.

faqs.q: How often should I update internal links on existing pages?
a: Every time you add a new page, check whether existing pages should link to it. And every time you update a page, check whether its existing internal links still point to the right targets. Beyond that, the 6-month full audit is sufficient for most sites.

faqs.q: What if a page cannot be fixed?
a: If a page genuinely cannot be indexed (e.g., it is behind a login wall or has a noindex tag), it should not be linked from the cluster in a way that suggests it is indexable. Either remove the links or redirect the page to a relevant alternative.

faqs.q: Should the audit be done by an SEO or by a developer?
a: Either can do the audit, but the fixes usually need developer involvement. An SEO can identify the issues (orphans, broken links, anchor problems) and recommend the fixes; a developer implements them if the CMS does not allow direct editing. For small sites with a simple CMS, one person can do both.

inline: Run the 8 steps, then the final checklist. If the checklist is satisfied, the cluster is structurally sound and ready for the long-term indexing phase. If not, fix the issues before moving on — structural problems compound, and they are much easier to fix now than after months of content has been built on top of them.
